transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-11
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sophie Chen (Redwood AE), Marco Patel (Redwood SE), Luis Ortega (Redwood SE), Aisha Khan (Veridian CTO), Tom Riley (Lead ML Eng), Mina Park (Infra), Jonas Weber (Product)

Auto-generated Summary: (may be imperfect)
- Veridian evaluating Redwood hosted vs dedicated vs private for conversational assistants and embedding search; major constraints are internal proxy, strict rate limits, and cost attribution per product.

Topics: SDKs, LangChain/LlamaIndex, gateway/proxy patterns, rate limits, observability hooks

--- Transcript ---
[00:00] Sophie (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for making time. quick intros? I'm Sophie, AE on the account, with Marco and Luis from our SE team.
[00:12] Aisha (Veridian): Hi, Aisha here, CTO. We have Tom, Mina and Jonas on the call. Thanks.
[00:18] Marco (Redwood SE): Great, thanks. Goal for today is to understand your integration surface — where you'll call Redwood from, whether behind a gateway, any SDK preferences like LangChain or LlamaIndex, and constraints like rate limits and observability.
[00:31] Tom (Veridian): Yeah, exactly. We're building a customer support assistant and embeddings-based search across docs. We want to know if we go hosted, can we still run our traffic through our API gateway so we keep auth and quota control.
[00:44] Luis (Redwood SE): Short answer is yes, you can proxy requests — many customers do an internal gateway that authenticates and then forwards to Redwood. We have examples for a gateway + token rotation pattern. Note though that if you proxy at scale you need to consider rate limiting at both sides.
[00:59] Mina (Veridian Infra): Our gateway injects a user context header and enforces per-customer quotas, we also have IP allowlists. Curious how Redwood handles those headers and whether we can preserve them for observability/cost attribution.
[01:14] Marco: You can forward headers; we can map those to metadata in our logs for per-route billing. There's some caveat—headers that are PII get redacted in logs by default, but you can configure metadata-only fields. (slight pause) sorry mic cut —
[01:27] Aisha: mic dropped, but got it. On the SDK side, Tom's been prototyping with LangChain and LlamaIndex. Are those supported out of the box?
[01:39] Marco: We have first-class SDKs in Python, Node, and go, and we maintain adapter snippets for LangChain and LlamaIndex. The LangChain connector is — hmm — I think the example in our repo is named redwood-cli-adapter, but the gist is that you can call our REST/HTTP endpoints or use our SDK client which handles streaming, retry logic, and built-in batching.
[01:58] Tom: When you say built-in batching, is that on the client side or the Redwood runtime does continuous batching? Because we care about latency for chat messages.
[02:09] Luis: Runtime does continuous batching server-side. The SDK also has optional client-side batching for high-throughput background jobs like embeddings. For chat we recommend streaming with small max tokens to keep latency low. There's some tradeoff: batching improves cost but can increase p99 latency.
[02:24] Jonas (Product): If we go dedicated, can we pin a model and avoid cross-tenant throttling?
[02:30] Marco: Yes, Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools and you can pin versions. It also gives you isolation on throughput; you still manage quotas at your side but Redwood will enforce per-customer rate limits to prevent noisy neighbor issues if you share a pool in some configs.
[02:43] Tom: About private deployments — we might need VPC or on-prem later. How much difference is there in the integration? Does the SDK need to change?
[02:53] Luis: For Private (VPC/on-prem) the SDK calls are identical — it's just the endpoint URL and auth tokens. For on-prem air-gapped installs you may run our runtime inside your network and we provide a private control plane. There are extra steps for KMS/HSM integration and audit logging but the surface for app devs is the same.
[03:09] Mina: Good to hear. On rate limits: we have strict per-user and per-team quotas. Do you support dynamic quotas via an API so we can update rules on the fly?
[03:21] Marco: We expose quota controls in the console for typical cases and have an API for programmatic quota updates for enterprise customers. For Dedicated we can also map your internal tenant identifier to Redwood API keys so your internal quota enforcement dovetails with Redwood's.
[03:35] Aisha: Observability — we need tracing across the call path. Can we pass trace IDs and see them in Redwood traces?
[03:42] Luis: Yes, you can forward trace headers (e.g., W3C traceparent). We ingest them and surface them in our trace view. There's a retention/PII policy, and sampling settings you can configure. Also, we provide per-route latency and token breakdowns in the Console.
[03:57] Tom: If we proxy, where do we run cost attribution? We want to attribute tokens per product line.
[04:03] Marco: Two common patterns: 1) Inject a product_id header at the gateway and have Redwood map that to a project; 2) Use separate API keys for each product line. Mapping headers requires you to whitelist allowed keys to avoid spoofing; using separate keys is simpler for accounting but more key management.
[04:22] Jonas: Any limits on header size or number? Our gateway adds ~8 custom headers.
[04:27] Luis: No hard limit on headers but logs will only index a subset. We can configure metadata fields you want to index.
[04:35] Aisha: Let's talk about LangChain/LlamaIndex specifics — we use LlamaIndex for our vector db pipeline. We currently generate embeddings with an internal model, but want to evaluate Redwood's embedding endpoints. Is the embeddings API stable? Any batch endpoints?
[04:50] Marco: Yes, embeddings are stable. We have an embeddings batch endpoint and the SDK supports batching with configurable batch sizes. There is also prefix/KV cache in the runtime for chat, but for embeddings it's pretty straightforward — send vectors, get back the embeddings. We also provide deterministic (non-stochastic) settings so you get consistent embeddings.
[05:06] Tom: When running through LlamaIndex, do you have a connector or example?
[05:10] Marco: We have a LlamaIndex adapter in our samples repo. It uses the SDK's embeddings client and shows the recommended chunking and batching pattern. We'll share that link.
[05:18] Sophie: I'll add that to the follow-ups. Next, about rate limit behaviors: if we hit a quota, do you return 429 with retry-after? Any idempotency considerations?
[05:30] Luis: We return 429 with Retry-After. For streaming completions we have partial responses + a final error event. We also provide leaky-bucket style rate limiting and quota windows configurable by customers on enterprise plans.
[05:43] Aisha: Security/compliance — do you have SOC2, encryption at rest, and KMS integrations?
[05:49] Marco: We are SOC 2 Type II and support KMS integrations for Private deployments. For hosted we use encryption at rest with customer-managed keys via BYOK in some tiers. We'll send the security one-pager.
[05:59] Tom: One practical point — our infra team requires an allowlist of IP ranges. Can you provide static egress IPs for hosted?
[06:07] Luis: For hosted we support customer-level IP allowlists and can provide a set of egress IPs per region, but for high availability that's a range. For strict allowlist customers, Dedicated or Private is recommended.
[06:20] Mina: For the technical deep-dive, we'd like to run a perf benchmark: sample traffic replay of 100 concurrent chat users, measure p50/p95/p99 with our prompts and pinned model. What's typical turnaround for a benchmark run?
[06:35] Marco: We can do an initial perf run within 7 business days for hosted; Dedicated benchmarking requires a little more coordination but we can run a smoke test quickly and then a formal benchmark once you share prompts and model choices. We'll need sample traffic, prompt sets, and desired SLAs.
[06:51] Jonas: Any differences in observability hooks between hosted and dedicated?
[06:56] Marco: Mostly the same APIs and trace formats. Dedicated gives you longer retention windows and the option to ship logs to your SIEM. Private offers the most flexibility: logs never leave your VPC unless you opt in.
[07:07] Aisha: Pricing — high level, we need per-token pricing and an idea for dedicated commit levels. We also want to understand what the minimum commit is for Dedicated.
[07:16] Sophie: I'll send the hosted per-token pricing and an example Dedicated commit schedule. Typical Dedicated minimums vary by region, but I'll include a few examples and the upgrade path.
[07:24] Tom: How do upgrades/rollouts work if we pin a model and a regression is detected? Can we auto-fallback?
[07:31] Marco: You can configure rollouts and automatic fallback policies in the console. We support canary rollouts and automatic fallback to a previous model version on metric regressions.
[07:40] Aisha: Good. Anything we should watch out for when putting Redwood behind our gateway?
[07:46] Luis: One thing is to ensure you propagate user identifiers and trace IDs consistently. Also be careful with client-side caching — for chat streaming you want to use token limits instead of large HTTP timeouts.
[07:59] Tom: On the SDK, streaming with server-sent events or WebSockets — what's supported?
[08:04] Marco: SDK supports HTTP streaming (EventStream / SSE) and WebSockets for low-latency streaming. For most web apps SSE is simpler.
[08:11] Jonas: Are there client libraries for TypeScript that support the same streaming semantics?
[08:15] Luis: Yes, our Node SDK exposes the same streaming API and an event emitter pattern.
[08:19] Aisha: Ok good. Let's switch to a quick POC checklist — what would you need from us to scope a 2-week POC?
[08:27] Marco: For a 2-week POC we'd want: 1) sample prompt sets and expected SLAs; 2) a small dataset for embeddings and recall tests; 3) a list of traffic patterns and desired concurrency; 4) whether you'll run through gateway or direct connections; 5) access to a contact for infra coordination.
[08:46] Mina: We can provide those. We'll need an NDA before sharing any sensitive prompt sets?
[08:51] Sophie: We have an NDA template; I'll attach it with the security docs. Usually basic non-disclosure is fine for POC data, but we can escalate if needed.
[08:59] Tom: Any caveats around tokenization differences if we compare to other vendors? We use some custom token accounting.
[09:06] Marco: Tokenization can vary by tokenizer. We provide a tokenization tool in the SDK and you'll see our token accounting in logs. For exact parity you'd run our tokenization as part of your preprocessing.
[09:17] Aisha: Final quick recaps and owners?
[09:20] Sophie: Recap — Sophie sends pricing + security + NDA; Marco sends LangChain/LlamaIndex examples, embeddings adapter, perf checklist; Mina to share gateway constraints. We'll schedule a technical deep-dive next week for the perf run.
[09:33] Aisha: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
[09:36] Sophie: Thanks all — we'll follow up with links and timing.
[09:40] End of call.
